processing: Sun-dried large-leaf maocha from the Menghai area goes through wo dui pile fermentation, typically lasting about two months for ripe pu-erh, and is then usually pressed.
harvest_season: Varies by maker; as with other ripe pu-erh it is often a blend of pickings, and some cakes are marketed on an early spring picking.
appearance_dry: Dark reddish-brown pressed leaf, often with golden tips scattered on the surface of better cakes.
appearance_wet: Soft dark chestnut leaf with some stem, typical of blended factory ripe tea.
taste_profile: Thick and mellow with sweetness and an aged, slightly savoury note that drinkers call the Menghai taste; some find older lots stemmy and musty.

brewing.notes: Typical of ripe pu-erh: boiling water and a quick rinse, then short early steeps. Break the cake gently to keep the leaf whole.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, usually as 357 g cakes or smaller formats, with factory teas also identified by recipe number and batch. As with other ripe pu-erh it is ready to drink when sold and is commonly bought at 1 to 10 years old. Menghai on the wrapper is a claim about place that only the maker can back up, so a known factory or a seller who names the source matters.
description:
This is ripe pu-erh tied to Menghai County in Xishuangbanna, the place most closely linked with the factory style of shu. The name is a looser label than a true appellation: it covers factory classics and small makers' cakes alike, as long as the leaf or the fermentation is said to be from Menghai.

The method is the usual wo dui, with local sun-dried large-leaf tea piled and fermented for a couple of months. Fans argue that local climate, leaf and long practice with piling together give a recognisable result, though that is drinkers' opinion rather than a measured fact.

In the cup it should be thick, sweet and calm, with a faintly savoury aged smell that people call Menghai wei. Brew it like any ripe tea, in boiling water with a fast rinse. If the first steeps smell of the pile, give it a few more or let the cake air for a while.

The benchmark is recipe 7572 from the Menghai Tea Factory, widely treated as the reference point for ripe tea and an easy way to learn what the style is about. Compare any other Menghai shu against it. Be wary of cakes that use the name without saying who made them, and of romantic labels such as 'early spring', which tell you little about the blend inside.
history:
Menghai's name in ripe tea rests on the Menghai Tea Factory, which took up the wo dui process soon after the Kunming Tea Factory developed it in 1973 and worked on the technique further. Recipe 7572 is said by sellers to date from the 1970s, though firm documentation of the recipe's early years is scarce.

Little is documented about Menghai shu as a separate style. The label appears mainly on factory and shop teas, and the general pu-erh rules are the only framework known to apply to it.
